mcqs.question: Why might a security team deploy a new detection rule in IDS mode before promoting it to IPS mode?
options: A false positive in IPS mode blocks live traffic and can cause an outage, so proving the rule is reliable in alert-only mode first limits that risk
IPS mode requires a separate certificate infrastructure that IDS does not
IDS devices are always cheaper to license than IPS devices
IDS mode can detect attacks that IPS mode is physically unable to see
mcqs.explanation: Because IPS sits inline and acts automatically, an untested rule that misfires on legitimate traffic becomes a self-inflicted outage — running it as IDS first surfaces false positives with zero traffic impact. Licensing cost, certificate infrastructure, and detection visibility aren't what differs between the two modes; the same detection logic can typically run in either.

mcqs.question: A zero-day exploit with no prior public disclosure is used against your network. Which detection approach is fundamentally unable to catch it by design, and why?
options: Anomaly-based detection, because it only works against known malware families
Host-based detection, because it cannot observe network traffic at all
Both approaches are equally unable to detect any zero-day exploit
Signature-based detection, because it matches traffic against known-bad patterns and a zero-day has no existing signature yet
mcqs.explanation: Signature-based detection is precise but only as good as its signature database — a genuinely novel attack has nothing to match against. Anomaly-based detection can potentially flag it by deviation from baseline even without a signature, and host-based detection is a different axis (network vs. host visibility) unrelated to signature vs. anomaly.

mcqs.question: A small spoofed DNS query triggers a much larger response sent to a victim who never made the request. What category of DDoS attack is this?
options: Application-layer (L7) attack
Volumetric attack via amplification/reflection
Protocol attack via SYN flood
Signature-evasion attack
mcqs.explanation: This is a reflection/amplification technique — a small spoofed request generates a disproportionately large response directed at the victim, multiplying the attacker's effective bandwidth, which is a volumetric attack pattern. A SYN flood targets connection-tracking state rather than amplifying response size, L7 attacks target expensive endpoints directly, and 'signature-evasion' isn't a DDoS category.

mcqs.question: A service has strong scrubbing-center and anycast protection at the network edge, but no application-layer defenses. What attack would still likely succeed?
options: A multi-terabit volumetric flood aimed at saturating bandwidth
A SYN flood exhausting connection-tracking tables
A DNS amplification attack reflecting traffic through open resolvers
A low-volume flood of well-formed requests against an expensive, unauthenticated search endpoint
mcqs.explanation: Network-layer defenses see and absorb volume and protocol-level attacks fine, but they can't distinguish a legitimate-looking, individually-cheap-to-pass HTTP request from an abusive one hammering an expensive endpoint — that requires application-layer defenses like rate limiting or caching. Volumetric, SYN-flood, and amplification attacks are exactly what network-layer defenses are built to catch.

mcqs.question: Why is it a mistake to judge DDoS risk purely by how much bandwidth an attacker could plausibly generate?
options: Because application-layer attacks can take a service down with a comparatively tiny volume of requests if those requests are individually expensive to serve
Because DDoS attacks always target bandwidth exclusively and never anything else
Because bandwidth-based attacks stopped being technically possible after IPv6 adoption
Because scrubbing centers make bandwidth irrelevant for every type of attack
mcqs.explanation: A few thousand requests per second against an unindexed query can exhaust database resources while barely registering on a bandwidth graph — bandwidth capacity says nothing about per-request cost. DDoS attacks aren't exclusively bandwidth-based, IPv6 didn't eliminate volumetric attacks, and scrubbing centers address volume, not L7 request cost.

mcqs.question: A team treats "our IDS fired an alert" as equivalent to "the attack was stopped." What's wrong with that reasoning?
options: IDS alerts are only informational metadata and cannot indicate a real attack
IDS systems only work on encrypted traffic, so unencrypted attacks wouldn't be alerted on anyway
By definition an IDS doesn't block traffic — the traffic that triggered the alert already reached its destination while the alert was generated and reviewed
IPS and IDS use identical detection logic, so the distinction doesn't matter
mcqs.explanation: IDS is a detection capability, not a blocking one — the traffic already passed through before anyone reviewed the alert, so treating detection as equivalent to prevention leaves the actual response gap unaddressed, especially outside business hours. IDS alerts are meaningful, not just metadata; IDS works on encrypted or unencrypted traffic depending on visibility, and IDS/IPS do differ meaningfully, not just in name.
